questions.question: What is the main practical downside of SPHINCS+ compared to ECDSA/Ed25519?
options: Much larger signatures
Much larger public keys
It requires trusted setup
It cannot be verified without the private key
questions.explanation: SPHINCS+ is designed to be conservative and stateless, but signatures are much larger than classical signatures.

questions.question: In a Merkle authentication path, what does the verifier need (besides the leaf value and its index) to recompute the root?
options: The sibling nodes along the path to the root
All leaves in the tree
The signer’s secret seed
The full internal tree structure in memory
questions.explanation: An auth path is exactly the sequence of sibling hashes needed to fold the leaf up to the root.

questions.question: Why does WOTS+ verification not require the signer’s secret key material?
options: The verifier can hash the revealed chain elements forward to the public key
The verifier can invert the hash function to recover the secret
The verifier guesses the missing chain links by brute force
The verifier replaces hashing with modular arithmetic
questions.explanation: A WOTS+ signature reveals intermediate chain values; verification completes the remaining hash steps to reconstruct the public key.

questions.question: In this lesson’s XMSS signature representation, what are the three main components?
options: (leaf_index, wots_sig, auth_path)
(pub_seed, secret_key, auth_path)
(root, pub_seed, signature_hash)
(nonce, commitment, challenge)
questions.explanation: XMSS signs with one WOTS+ key at a chosen leaf and proves that leaf is in the XMSS Merkle tree via an authentication path.

questions.question: What does SPHINCS+ gain by stacking XMSS trees into a hypertree?
options: Many more one-time keys can be used under a single top-level public root
Smaller signatures than a single XMSS tree
A requirement for synchronized signer state across devices
Deterministic signatures without hashing
questions.explanation: The hypertree lets you authenticate many XMSS subtrees: a lower-layer root is signed by an upper layer, chaining up to one public root.

questions.question: In our toy `sphincs_verify`, why can the verifier compute a bottom XMSS root candidate without knowing any bottom private seeds?
options: The bottom XMSS root is computed from the bottom signature itself (implicit verification)
The bottom XMSS root is included verbatim in the public key
The bottom XMSS root is always all-zero bytes
The verifier downloads the bottom seeds from a key server
questions.explanation: An XMSS signature plus message lets the verifier reconstruct a candidate XMSS root; higher layers then authenticate that root up to the trusted public root.

questions.question: Which implementation mistake most directly enables forgeries in one-time or few-time hash-based signatures?
options: Reusing the same one-time key (or leaf index) to sign multiple messages
Using SHA-256 instead of SHA-512
Storing the public key in hex instead of bytes
Choosing a taller Merkle tree than necessary
questions.explanation: If the same one-time key is used twice, the attacker may combine revealed information from both signatures to forge additional signatures.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of domain separation / addressing in hash-based signature schemes?
options: Ensure hashes used for different roles (leaves, parents, chains, PRFs) don’t collide by construction
Make signatures smaller by compressing hashes
Allow the verifier to skip checking authentication paths
Make the hash function invertible for verification
questions.explanation: By mixing role-specific tags and addresses into hash inputs, you reduce the risk that a value meant for one role is valid in another.
